rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders latif as unfathomable; here it underscores that judgment about what happens belongs only to God.
rows.anchor: this term supplies a further accent, as it were, on the theme "judgment as to what is to happen rests with none but God"

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'of dominion' indicates that absolute power and dominion belong to God alone.
rows.anchor: absolute power and absolute dominion belong to God alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the meaning of ta'wil, Asad refers readers to his note on 12:6.
rows.anchor: See note 10 on verse 6 of this surah.

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the phrase literally as 'with them.'
rows.anchor: Lit., "with them".

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.
Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Basirah derives from seeing and means seeing with the mind, or understanding founded on conscious insight.
rows.anchor: the noun basirah (as also the verb) has the abstract connotation of "seeing with one's mind"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term can also mean evidence accessible to, or verifiable by, the intellect.
rows.anchor: an evidence accessible to the intellect" or "verifiable by the intellect"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's call rests on reason-verifiable insight, expressing the Qur'an's approach to faith, ethics, and morality and recurring calls to reason and thought.
rows.anchor: the outcome of a conscious insight accessible to, and verifiable by, man's reason

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This answers unbelievers who object that a mortal like themselves could not have been entrusted with God's message.
rows.anchor: a mortal like themselves could not have been entrusted with God's message to man

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hatta means 'until' and links the verse to earlier apostles; Zamakhshari understands that they suffered long before God vindicated them.
rows.anchor: the implication being (according to Zamakhshari) that they used to suffer for a long time before they were vindicated by God

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: 'They had been given the lie' may mean the people dismissed the apostles' hope of God's help as wishful thinking, or reality seemed to refute their expectation of speedy help.
rows.anchor: either by their people, who regarded the apostles' expectation of God's succour as mere wishful thinking, or by the harsh reality

rows.speaker: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn 'Abbas cited 2:214 to illustrate the distress of the apostle and believers asking when God's succour would come.
rows.anchor: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas used to quote 2:214 - "so shaken were they that the apostle, and the believers with him, would exclaim, 'When will God's succour come?"

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Their stories' means the stories of the prophets.
rows.anchor: Lit., "in their stories" - i.e., the stories of the prophets

rows.speaker: Baghawi and Zamakhshari
rows.claim: They take the reference to the discourse as referring to the Qur'an as a whole; the following passage connects with 12:102-105.
rows.anchor: the Qur'an as a whole (Baghawi and Zamakhshari). The passage that follows connects with verses 102-105

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle 'but' here marks the impossibility that Muhammad invented the revelation.
rows.anchor: denoting here the impossibility of its having been invented by Muhammad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Everything' means everything a person may need for spiritual welfare; Asad also points to 10:37 and note 60.
rows.anchor: everything that man may need for his spiritual welfare. See also 10:37 and the corresponding note 60

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Inviolable House is the Ka'bah, whose prototype is attributed to Abraham and which is called the first temple for worship of the One God.
rows.anchor: the Temple of the Ka'bah, the prototype of which owed its origin to Abraham

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Remote House denotes Solomon's ancient temple or its site and symbolizes the line of Hebrew prophets; the two sanctuaries show Islam's message continues and develops the same divine religion.
rows.anchor: The juxtaposition of these two sacred temples is meant to show that the Qur'an does not inaugurate a "new" religion but represents a continuation and the ultimate development of the same divine message

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ayah primarily means a sign or token by which something is known, though the Qur'an often uses it for a divine message.
rows.anchor: by which a thing is known

rows.speaker: Raghib
rows.claim: Raghib defines ayah as any perceivable phenomenon connected with something not itself similarly perceivable; min ayatina therefore suggests insight into ultimate truths through symbols.
rows.anchor: any perceivable phenomenon (irrespective of whether it is apparent to the senses or only to the intellect) connected with a thing

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening 'And' presents the Night Journey and Ascension as divine grace of the same high order as revelation to Moses, whose direct speech from God is cited in 4:164 and 7:143-144.
rows.anchor: meant to show that the mystic Night Journey - and, by implication, the subsequent Ascension as well - were experiences of the same high order of divine grace

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hebrew religious history is repeatedly cited because revelations to its prophets were monotheism's earliest formulation and thus important to its later development.
rows.anchor: the revelations granted to their prophets represent the earliest formulation of monotheism, which makes it ideologically important for its later development

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wakil can mean a manager or one responsible for another's conduct; elsewhere it is rendered guardian, defender, or caretaker, while here and in 39:62 it means God's exclusive power to determine fate.
rows.anchor: in the present instance (as well as in 39:62) the term evidently alludes to God's exclusive power to determine the fate

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'In the revelation' is generic and probably refers to predictions in the Torah and prophecies of Isaiah, Jeremiah, John, and Jesus.
rows.anchor: here evidently used in the generic sense of the word, and probably applying to predictions contained in the Torah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because both Bible and Qur'an describe repeated Israelite rebellion, 'twice' most likely means two extended historical periods, not two isolated events.
rows.anchor: does not refer to two single instances but, rather, to two distinct, extended periods of their history

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibad means all created beings, here human agents subject to God's will; the warriors probably refer to Assyrians, Babylonians, or both, whose conquests form one period.
rows.anchor: relates to the Assyrians who overran Palestine in the seventh century B.C. and caused the disappearance of the greater part of the Hebrew nation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's sending tribulation on sinners is a metonym for cause and effect operating in individual and collective human life.
rows.anchor: God's "sending" tribulations upon reprobate sinners is here, as elsewhere in the Qur'an, a metonym for the natural law of cause and effect

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The restored turn against Israel apparently refers to Jewish return from Babylonian captivity, partial state restoration, and rebuilding a temple in the late sixth century BCE.
rows.anchor: the return of the Jews from the Babylonian captivity in the last quarter of the sixth century B.C., the partial re-establishment of their state

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Evil to your faces' uses the face for the whole person and means utter disgrace; the passage probably refers to Titus's destruction of the Second Temple and Jewish state in 70 CE.
rows.anchor: the "evil done to one's face" is synonymous with "utter disgrace". Most probably, this passage relates to the destruction

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.
Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Most upright' means ethical rectitude and benefit to individual and social life; the passage returns to God's guidance through prophetic revelation, first raised in verse 2.
rows.anchor: conformable to ethical rectitude and beneficial to man's individual and social life

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this context, Asad takes the conjunction wa to mean 'as it is.'
rows.anchor: This, to my mind, is the meaning of the conjunctive particle wa in the above context

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast in 2:216 shows that divine guidance is the only objective criterion of good and bad.
rows.anchor: in other words, divine guidance is the only objective criterion as to what is good and what is bad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ayatayn means two symbols of spiritual darkness and light, as the following clause indicates.
rows.anchor: the expression ayatayn ("two symbols") refers - as the subsequent clause shows - to the symbols of spiritual darkness and light

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The daylight symbol is the Qur'anic message leading people from spiritual ignorance and error into faith and reason.
rows.anchor: the message of the Qur'an, which is meant to lead man out of spiritual ignorance and error into the light of faith and reason

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The count of years also means the years of one's own life, calling for spiritual self-criticism in light of life's brevity.
rows.anchor: it obviously implies here a call to spiritual self-criticism in view of the ephemeral nature of one's worldly life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Everything' means what people need in ethics and religion.
rows.anchor: everything that man may be in need of in the domain of ethics and religion

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ta'ir literally means bird or flying creature and became a term for omen, fortune, or destiny because Arabs read the future from birds' flight.
rows.anchor: the term ta'ir came to be tropically used in the sense of "fortune", both good and evil, or "destiny"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'anic destiny concerns the moral direction a person chooses, not chiefly external events; inclinations, attitudes, actions, and omissions shape one's spiritual fate, for which God holds each person responsible.
rows.anchor: man's spiritual fate depends on himself and is inseparably linked with the whole tenor of his personality

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: The record and account allegorize a person's full comprehension of their past life on Judgment Day; related images appear in 37:19, 39:68, and 50:22.
rows.anchor: represent man's total comprehension, on Judgment Day, of all his past life (Razi). This allegory occurs in the Qur'an in many formulations

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The principle that each person bears only their own burden is also stated in 6:164, 35:18, 39:7, and 53:38; Asad calls 53:38 the earliest Qur'anic statement of this ethic.
rows.anchor: also 53:38, which represents the earliest Qur'anic statement of this fundamental principle of ethics

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apostle is sent so the community can understand right and wrong; Asad links this with 6:131-132 and 29:59, which chronologically precedes this surah.
rows.anchor: so that they might fully understand the meaning of right and wrong

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Our command' means a final warning to mend ways; qaryah, literally town, usually denotes a community or its people.
rows.anchor: The term qaryak (ht., "town") denotes usually - though not always - a "community" or "people of a community"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mutraf refers to people who pursue pleasures without moral concern; their wealth and social position make them community leaders morally responsible for followers.
rows.anchor: those who, by virtue of their wealth and social position, embody the real leadership of their community and are, therefore, morally responsible

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.
Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means assigning hell to a person.
rows.anchor: shall assign"] hell to him

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here 'believer' entails recognizing God's absolute oneness and willingly accepting guidance through prophetic revelation, since striving for the hereafter presupposes belief and accountability.
rows.anchor: the term "believer" relates, in this context, to a cognition of God's absolute oneness and uniqueness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the Arabic sentence is singular before the final clause, Asad renders the pronouns in the plural to match that clause and normal Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: in view of the next clause, which is expressed in the plural, it is preferable to render these pronouns

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tafdilan means a greater bestowal of bounty, but here also includes merit, supporting a combined translation.
rows.anchor: the latter term obviously comprises, in this instance, the concept of "merit" as well

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari and Razi
rows.claim: God is the ultimate cause of human life while parents are its immediate outward cause, which explains the injunction to honor them.
rows.anchor: his parents are its outward, immediate cause: and so the preceding call to God is followed by the injunction to honour and cherish one's parents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage through 17:39 makes kindness and just dealings between people integral to striving for the good of the hereafter.
rows.anchor: kindness and just dealings between man and man are an integral part of the concept of "striving for the good of the life to come"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Uff is an Arabic word or sound expressing contempt, dislike, or disgust.
rows.anchor: In Arabic, uff - a word or sound indicative of contempt, dislike or disgust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image of lowering a wing in tenderness evokes a bird lovingly spreading its wings over its young in the nest.
rows.anchor: a bird that lovingly spreads its wings over its offspring in the nest

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's bracketed phrase supplies the implied sense of the elliptical sentence, following Tabari, Baghawi, Zamakhshari, and Razi.
rows.anchor: This interpolation gives the meaning of the above elliptic sentence (Tabari, Baghawi Zamakhshari, Razi)

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari and Razi
rows.claim: The due owed to relatives here is loving consideration; needy relatives are included in the following category of the needy.
rows.anchor: "his due" evidently refers to the loving consideration due to one's relatives (Zamakhshari and Razi)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the expression 'wayfarer,' Asad refers readers to surah 2, note 145.
rows.anchor: Regarding this expression, see surah 2, note 145

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabdhir means squandering for no good purpose, so the prohibition concerns why one spends rather than how much.
rows.anchor: the term tabdhir does not relate to the quantity but, rather, to the purpose of one's spending

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud
rows.claim: They define tabdhir as spending without a righteous purpose or for a frivolous, false cause.
rows.anchor: Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud (both of them quoted by Tabari) defined tabdhir as "spending without a righteous purpose"

rows.speaker: Mujahid
rows.claim: Mujahid says spending all one's wealth on a righteous cause is not squandering, while even a small sum spent frivolously is.
rows.anchor: Mujahid is reported (ibid.) to have said, "If a man were to spend all that he possesses in a righteous cause, it could not be termed squandering

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because squandering shows ingratitude for God's sustenance, squanderers are called brethren of satans; Asad refers to his note on 15:16 for satanic terminology.
rows.anchor: squandering - in the sense explained in the preceding note - implies an utter lack of gratitude for the gift of sustenance bestowed by God

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning away from people in need means that one is oneself needy and unable to help them.
rows.anchor: because thou art thyself in want, and therefore unable to help others

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition may address pre-Islamic killing of unwanted girls and rarer sacrifices of boys, but timelessly forbids abortions undertaken solely for economic fear of poverty.
rows.anchor: the above prohibition has a timeless validity inasmuch as it relates also to abortions undertaken "for fear of poverty", i.e., on purely economic grounds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command not to come near zina intensifies the ban; zina covers any sex between a man and woman who are not married to each other, whether either is married elsewhere, including adultery and fornication.
rows.anchor: the term zina signifies all sexual intercourse between a man and a woman who are not husband and wife, irrespective of whether either of them is married to another partner

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Killing by right includes execution of a legal sentence, a just war, or legitimate individual self-defense.
rows.anchor: in the execution of a legal sentence or in a just war

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.
Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qisas is the legal punishment for homicide; the protector is usually the victim's heir or next of kin.
rows.anchor: the term wall ("protector" or "defender of [one's] rights") is usually taken to mean the heir or next of kin of the victim

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: The protector may also be the government, understood as defender of every citizen's rights.
rows.anchor: it may also apply to the government (as-sultan): an interpretation which is obviously based on the concept of the government

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wrongful killing means intentional homicide, because Qur'anic zulm applies to intentional rather than accidental wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: the concept of zulm applies in the Qur'an exclusively to intentional and never to accidental wrongdoing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A court may sentence only the actual murderer and may recognize mitigating circumstances or forgo capital punishment altogether.
rows.anchor: not entitled to impose a capital sentence on any but the actual murderer or murderers

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: The slain person is avenged by retribution in this life and receives special divine grace in the hereafter.
rows.anchor: he is avenged in this world by the retribution exacted from his murderer, and in the life to come, blessed by the special grace

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: Alternatively, 'he' means the victim's protector or heir, who is sufficiently supported by qisas and should not demand excess punishment.
rows.anchor: relate the pronoun "he" to the defender of the victim's rights, respectively, to the latter's heir or next of kin

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the instruction about an orphan's property, Asad refers to his note on 6:152.
rows.anchor: See surah 6, note 149

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic says literally that every promise will be asked about or investigated.
rows.anchor: every promise shall be asked about" or "investigated"

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mustaqim, 'straight,' has a moral or spiritual sense in the Qur'an, so fair weights apply to every human dealing, not only commerce; compare 6:152.
rows.anchor: the above injunction applies not merely to commercial transactions but to all dealings between man and man

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command can mean not to pursue what one lacks knowledge of, including slander or false testimony, unsupported guesses, and interference in social matters one cannot assess.
rows.anchor: groundless assertions about events or people (and hence to slander or false testimony), to statements based on guesswork unsupported by evidence

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators limit the condemnation to the conduct in the two immediately preceding verses.
rows.anchor: this condemnation refers to what has been mentioned in the preceding two verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad prefers to read the condemnation as covering all prohibitions, explicit or implied, in 17:22-37.
rows.anchor: more probably, however, it extends to the subject-matter of all the prohibitions - whether enunciated as such or merely implied - in verses 22-37

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hikmah may mean revealed wisdom; from hakama, 'prevent or restrain,' it first means what prevents evil or ignorance, and positively means conscious insight into excellence.
rows.anchor: the primary meaning of hikmah is "that which prevents one from evil or ignorant behaviour"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here hikmah implies human moral discernment and presupposes an absolute standard of values willed by God.
rows.anchor: it implies moral discrimination (or "the knowledge of right and wrong") on the part of men; and this, in its turn, presupposes the existence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Absolute moral values independent of time and society require belief in God and final judgment; the passage therefore closes as it opened with God's oneness.
rows.anchor: the passage ends, as it began. with a call to a cognition of God's oneness and uniqueness

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse alludes to Arabs who treated angels as female sub-deities or God's daughters despite contempt for daughters; the rhetorical question exposes the absurdity of sharing divinity with any being.
rows.anchor: the pre-Islamic Arabian belief that the angels - conceived of as a kind of female sub-deities - were God's "daughters"

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arsh means God's absolute sway, so dhu al-arsh is 'He enthroned in His almightiness.'
rows.anchor: the term 'arsh (lit., "throne" or, more properly, "seat of power") is used in the Qur'an to denote God's absolute sway

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: One interpretation is that rival deities would try to seize God's power and thereby create universal chaos.
rows.anchor: they would endeavour to deprive Him of some or all of His power, and would thus create chaos in the universe

rows.speaker: Tabari and Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: Asad favors their argument: alleged divine mediators would themselves acknowledge dependence on God, thereby negating their divinity and showing people should turn directly to Him.
rows.anchor: most prominently among them Tabari and Ibn Kathir - have a far better, though somewhat more complicated explanation to offer

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad refers readers to his note on 6:88 for this expression.
rows.anchor: See surah 6, note 88

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad refers readers to his note on 2:20 for 'the seven heavens.'
rows.anchor: For an explanation of this expression, see surah 2, note 20

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation testifies to a conscious creative will, but people are often blind and deaf to the evidence of God's ever-present power.
rows.anchor: everything in creation bears witness to the existence of a conscious Creative Will, man is only too often blind and deaf

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This passage connects with 17:41.
rows.anchor: This passage connects with verse 41 above

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad compares the veils over hearts and deafness with 6:25 and 2:7.
rows.anchor: Cf. 6:25. See also 2:7 and the corresponding note

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally says that the Prophet mentions his Sustainer alone in the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: Lit., "whenever thou dost mention in the Qur'an thy Sustainer alone"

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents listen in order to find fault with the Qur'anic message.
rows.anchor: I.e., to find fault with the message of the Qur'an

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.
Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase covers any created matter that seems even less capable of having or receiving life.
rows.anchor: even less susceptible of having or receiving life

rows.speaker: Tabari and Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Earthly life seems only brief beside the unlimited duration of the hereafter.
rows.anchor: Man's life on earth will appear to him "but as a little while" in comparison with the unlimited duration of the life in the hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concept of time is earthbound and has no meaning in ultimate reality; resurrected deniers will praise God because they then recognize His existence and almightiness.
rows.anchor: man's concept of "time" is earthbound and, hence, has no meaning in the context of ultimate reality

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad cross-references 16:125 and 29:46 on speaking kindly to people of different beliefs.
rows.anchor: Cf. 16:125 (and the corresponding note 149) as well as 29:46

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal wording says Satan stirs discord between people.
rows.anchor: Lit., "Satan stirs up discord between them"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For wakil here, Asad uses 'one who can determine another's fate,' as in his note on 17:2; he also accepts 'charged with responsibility for their conduct.'
rows.anchor: An alternative, equally acceptable rendering of the above phrase would be

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari and Baydawi
rows.claim: The prophets' differing degrees may allude to Muhammad's role as Last Prophet: he cannot determine his audience's fate, but his message will remain alive forever.
rows.anchor: an allusion to the role of Muhammad as the Last Prophet (Zamakhshari, Baydawi): despite his personal inability to "determine the fate"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As David's Psalms outlasted his kingdom, Muhammad's Qur'anic message will outlast the changing fortunes of its followers.
rows.anchor: David's "book of divine wisdom" (the Psalms) had outlived the glory of his earthly kingdom, so will Muhammad's message

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted words are 'to those who believe in the existence of any divine power apart from God.'
rows.anchor: to those who believe in the existence of any divine power apart from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence concerns worship directed to saints or angels.
rows.anchor: this relates to the worship of saints or angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shifting affliction onto themselves alludes to the Christian doctrine of vicarious atonement.
rows.anchor: to transfer it onto themselves: obviously an allusion to the Christian doctrine of "vicarious atonement"

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those nearest to God include the greatest prophets as well as angels.
rows.anchor: the greatest of the prophets, as well as the angels

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because everything worldly is temporary and perishes, people should remain conscious of the life to come.
rows.anchor: since everything in this world is ephemeral and bound to perish, man ought to be conscious of the life to come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The decree means God's immutable laws for creation.
rows.anchor: in accordance with the immutable laws which God has laid down for His creation

none: Translation only; no separate commentary point.
